definition: An inward shift shows a fall in productive capacity.
The next best alternative forgone when a decision is made.
example: The opportunity cost of producing an additional 100 units of capital goods is 200 units of consumer goods.

definition: An outward shift shows positive economic growth / a rise in productive capacity.
A point inside the PPC means resources are unemployed or underused.
A point on the PPC means resources are fully employed.
A point outside the PPC is unobtainable with current resources.
A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology.
The basic economic problem where limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants.
example: This moves the economy from PPF1 to PPF2 as more of both goods can now be produced.

definition: The satisfaction or usefulness a consumer gets from a good or service.
A firm or individual that makes goods or provides services.
When a firm aims to make as much profit as possible, where MC = MR.
The quantity of a good that consumers are willing and able to buy at various prices during a time period.
example: If cocoa bean prices fell from $3000 to $2000 per tonne, quantity demanded might rise from 1000 to 1500 tonnes.

definition: The demand curve shows the relationship between price and quantity demanded. An increase in demand shifts the curve right.
A change in price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift.
example: If cocoa bean prices fell from $3000 to $2000 per tonne, quantity demanded might rise from 1000 to 1500 tonnes.

definition: Advertising raises awareness so more consumers know about a product and demand increases.
example: Pepsi advertising during the Cricket World Cup raises brand awareness and shifts demand right.

definition: A good that is used together with another, so if the price of one rises, demand for the other falls.
When income rises, purchasing power increases, consumers can afford more, and demand for normal goods rises.
A good that can be used in place of another, so if the price of one rises, demand for the other increases.
A change in price causes a movement along the supply curve, not a shift.
example: If wheat prices rose from $200 to $250 per tonne, farmers would supply more wheat.

definition: The quantity of a good that producers are willing and able to sell at different prices.
example: If wheat prices rose from $200 to $250 per tonne, farmers would supply more wheat.

definition: A tax levied on goods and services, which increases production costs and reduces supply.
If costs rise, profit per unit falls, producers are less willing to sell, quantity supplied falls at each price, and supply falls.
A payment from the government to producers that reduces costs and increases supply.
If technology improves, output per worker rises, costs fall, more can be produced at each price, and supply rises.
The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, with no tendency to change.
When quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the current price, causing a shortage.
When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the current price, causing a surplus.
A shortage is excess demand: consumers cannot buy all they want at the current price.
A surplus is excess supply: unsold stock builds up at the current price.
A measure of how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price, calculated as percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
example: People driving to work every day keep buying petrol, so PED for petrol is inelastic.

definition: Demand is price elastic when PED is greater than 1, so a price rise cuts quantity demanded significantly and total revenue falls.
Price inelastic demand means PED is less than 1, so quantity changes proportionally less than price.
example: Petrol is essential for many commuters, so demand changes little when price rises.

definition: A measure of how responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price.
Price inelastic supply means PES is less than 1. Fresh fish spoils quickly and cannot be stored for long, so supply cannot rise quickly.
A good with negative YED: when income rises, consumers switch to better alternatives and demand for the inferior good falls.
A good with positive YED: when income rises, demand rises.
example: YED = 15% / 20% = 0.75. This is a normal good because YED is positive, and it is a necessity because YED is less than 1.

definition: A measure of how demand changes in response to a change in income.
Someone who benefits from a good without paying for it.
When the free market fails to allocate resources efficiently.
An economic system with both private sector and public sector involvement.
Owned by individuals / businesses.
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival, such as street lighting or defence.
Owned or funded by government.
Rivalry between firms trying to win customers.
A market with a single dominant seller.
example: The merged Vodafone-Idea company would have 40% market share and 400 million customers.

definition: The transfer of ownership of a business from the public sector to the private sector.
example: Austrian Railways may face new competitors after privatisation.

definition: A benefit received by a third party not involved in the economic activity, such as from education.
A cost imposed on a third party not involved in the economic activity, such as pollution.
Private benefit plus external benefit.
Private cost plus external cost.
Someone affected by a decision but not directly buying or selling the good.
Man-made aids to production such as machinery, tools, and buildings.
The factor that organises the other factors and takes risks in business decisions.
Human effort used in production, both physical and mental.
Raw materials (growing and collecting raw cotton).
Extraction and collection of raw materials, such as farming, fishing, and mining.
Manufacturing (turning cotton into a shirt).
Manufacturing and construction, turning raw materials into finished goods.
Provision of services such as retail, banking, education, and healthcare.
Breaking down production into separate tasks so workers can specialise.
Output per worker, usually measured as total output divided by number of workers.
The efficiency with which inputs are converted into outputs.
When workers or countries concentrate on producing what they are best at.
Total cost divided by output.
A cost that does not change with output, such as rent or salaries.
The difference between total revenue and total cost.
The sum of all costs incurred in production, including fixed and variable costs.
The total amount of money a firm receives from selling goods, calculated as price times quantity.
A cost that changes when output changes, such as raw materials.
When average costs rise as a firm grows too large.
When average costs fall as a firm increases its output.
Cost savings that come from the growth of the whole industry.
Cost savings that come from the growth of the firm itself.
A curve showing how average costs change as output increases in the long-run.
Obstacles that make it difficult for new firms to enter a market.
Rivalry between firms trying to attract customers and increase market share.
A market with many buyers and sellers where no single firm can influence price.
A firm that must accept the market price because it has no power to set its own price.
An increase in the size, output, or market share of a firm.
A business with high output, many employees, and significant market presence.
The percentage of total market sales held by one firm.
A business with low output, few employees, and often local market focus.
An obstacle that prevents new firms from entering a market.
A market structure with a single dominant seller.
Legal protection that gives a firm exclusive rights to produce a new invention.
A firm with enough market power to set its own price.
Obstacles that prevent new competitors from entering the market.
When firms cooperate, formally or informally, to fix prices or limit output.
When firms consider rivals' reactions before making decisions.
A market dominated by a few large firms that are interdependent.
The number of workers firms are willing to hire at different wage levels.
The wage rate where demand for labour equals supply of labour.
The number of workers willing to work at different wage levels.
Trade unions use collective bargaining power to negotiate higher wages; employers must agree or face strikes.
example: In the US textile industry, a large union can negotiate better terms for workers.

definition: An organisation that represents workers to improve wages and working conditions.
Action taken by the government to influence market outcomes.
The lowest legal wage rate that employers can pay workers.
Government rules that control how firms and individuals behave.
A government payment that reduces the cost of production or consumption.
A compulsory payment to government that raises revenue or discourages an activity.
A period of rapid economic growth with rising output and employment.
An increase in real GDP over time.
The total value of goods and services produced in an economy over a time period.
A period when real GDP falls for two consecutive quarters.
Consumer Price Index, a measure of inflation based on a basket of goods and services.
A sustained decrease in the general price level over time.
A sustained increase in the general price level over time.
example: Argentine consumers found their wages could not keep up with rising prices in December 2017.

definition: The cost of borrowing money or the return on saving.
Unemployment caused by a downturn in the economic cycle.
Short-term unemployment when workers are between jobs.
Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs.
People of working age who are willing and able to work but cannot find a job.
example: In South Africa, youth unemployment is especially severe, limiting future opportunities.

definition: A record of a country's trade in goods and services and income flows.
example: Indonesia's deficit reached 3% of GDP, putting pressure on the rupiah.

definition: When imports exceed exports, leading to a net outflow of money.
Goods and services sold to other countries.
Goods and services bought from other countries. When imports exceed exports there is a current account deficit.
When exports exceed imports, leading to a net inflow of money.
A tax that raises the cost of polluting so firms seek cleaner alternatives and pollution falls.
A cost to third parties not involved in the activity.
Government sets limits; firms must comply or face fines, so harmful activity decreases.
Low-income households receive support, purchasing power rises, and poverty falls.
An uneven distribution of income across households, which governments try to reduce by redistributing income.
Higher earners pay a larger share, government revenue rises, income is redistributed, and inequality falls.
When government spending is greater than tax revenue.
When tax revenue is greater than government spending.
Income households keep after taxes, which rises when taxes fall and can raise consumption.
Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation to influence economic activity.
example: The Slovenian government spent €3.05bn on healthcare in 2019, including extra funding to cut waiting times.

definition: The proportion of household disposable income that is saved rather than spent. It is usually expressed as saving as a percentage of disposable income.
example: Between January 2015 and July 2017, the UK savings ratio followed a downward overall trend, so households were saving a smaller share of their income by the end of the period.

definition: Total demand in the economy. Lower interest rates can raise borrowing and spending, so aggregate demand rises.
The institution that sets interest rates to control inflation.
The cost of borrowing money or the return on saving.
example: If interest rates rise, borrowing becomes more expensive, mortgages and loans cost more, consumption falls, and inflation falls.

definition: Monetary policy controls interest rates to influence inflation and economic growth.
example: China's central bank brought interest rates down to 4.35% when growth was slowing.

definition: Fewer rules to follow, so firms save time and money and efficiency rises.
Workers gain skills, productivity per worker rises, firms produce more, and output increases.
Policies that aim to increase productivity and long-run economic growth.
example: Ecuador claimed a 5.8% unemployment rate in October 2017 was the result of supply-side policies.

definition: The part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, plus net income and current transfers.
An increase in real GDP over time.
A sustained rise in the general price level.
When achieving one objective makes it harder to achieve another.
People of working age who are willing and able to work but cannot find a job.
Investment by a firm in production or business operations in another country.
The increasing interconnection and integration of economies around the world.
example: More production and transport may increase pollution.

definition: A business that operates in more than one country.
The reduction or removal of trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas.
Investment in productive business activity in another country.
The country receiving the investment.
An MNC enters a country, a factory is built, jobs are created, household incomes rise, and consumer spending rises.
A company with production or operations in more than one country.
Profits sent back to the company’s home country.
When a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country.
Goods and services sold to other countries.
Trade without tariffs, quotas, or other restrictions.
example: The TPP would have reduced tariffs across Pacific economies, making goods cheaper.

definition: Goods and services bought from other countries.
The exchange of goods and services between countries.
Selling goods in a foreign market below cost or below the home-market price.
A new domestic industry that may need temporary protection to grow.
Government action to restrict international trade to protect domestic industries.
example: Steel tariffs can save jobs in domestic steel mills.

definition: A legal limit on the quantity of imports allowed.
A tax on imported goods that raises their price.
A trading bloc with free trade between members and a common external tariff.
A group of countries with no tariffs between members.
When lower trade barriers allow countries to buy from lower-cost producers inside the bloc.
When trade shifts from a more efficient outside producer to a less efficient member country.
A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between themselves.
A product that has been processed or made in factories.
A raw material or natural product, such as coffee, oil, or copper.
A disagreement between countries over trade rules or restrictions.
An international organisation that promotes freer trade and resolves trade disputes.
An increase in the value of a currency.
The desire to buy a currency, usually to buy that country’s exports or invest there.
A decrease in the value of a currency. Depreciation means a fall in the value of the currency.
example: A weaker euro made German cars and machinery cheaper for foreign buyers and helped Germany's current account surplus.

definition: The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
The amount of a currency being sold, usually to buy imports or invest abroad.
An increase in the value of a currency.
A decrease in the value of a currency.
An official decrease in the value of a currency in a fixed exchange rate system.
An official increase in the value of a currency in a fixed exchange rate system.
